sources.name: Musées de la Ville de Strasbourg
Office de Tourisme du Pays de Saverne

sights.n: Place Stanislas, Place de la Carrière & Place d'Alliance
sights.w: Nancy's UNESCO-listed ensemble (since 1983) and one of the most harmonious urban compositions of the Enlightenment: the gilded 18th-century royal square built 1752-1756 for Duke Stanislas Leszczynski by architect Emmanuel Héré, with Jean Lamour's wrought-iron gates and gilded fountains, linked by the tree-lined Place de la Carrière to the smaller Place d'Alliance. The masterpiece of the ducal city.

sights.address: 36-38 Rue du Sergent Blandan, 54000 Nancy, France
sights.w: The temple of Nancy Art Nouveau — the only museum in France devoted to the École de Nancy movement led by Émile Gallé, Louis Majorelle, the Daum brothers and Jacques Gruber. Set in a 1900s villa with fully furnished rooms, glass, furniture, ceramics, stained glass and a garden, it makes the case for Nancy as Art Nouveau's second capital after Brussels.

The first wholly Art Nouveau house in Nancy, designed 1901-1902 by Henri Sauvage for cabinetmaker Louis Majorelle — a total artwork uniting Majorelle's ironwork and furniture, Jacques Gruber's stained glass and Alexandre Bigot's stoneware. Labelled a 'Maison des Illustres' and reopened after restoration, it is the only Art Nouveau house in the city open to visitors year-round.

sights.n: Palais des Ducs de Lorraine – Musée Lorrain
sights.w: The former palace of the Dukes of Lorraine in the Ville-Vieille, its late-15th-century Porterie one of the first Renaissance works in eastern France. The Musée Lorrain inside holds over 150,000 works telling Lorraine's history from prehistory to today, spread across the ducal palace, its garden and the adjoining Cordeliers church and convent.

On Place Stanislas itself, one of France's oldest fine-art museums (founded 1793): European painting from the 14th century to now, a strong Lorraine collection, and a spectacular basement gallery of Daum glass built into the city's medieval fortifications.

sights.address: Rue de la Craffe, 54000 Nancy, France
sights.w: The twin-towered 14th-century gate that guarded the northern entrance to Nancy's old town until 1610, through which the Dukes of Lorraine made their entry — the most striking surviving remnant of the medieval city walls.

A neo-Gothic jewel in the heart of the Ville-Vieille, built 1864-1871 by architect Prosper Morey with stained glass from the Carl Geyling workshops and altars donated by kings and emperors. Its soaring spire is a landmark of old Nancy.

Nancy's beloved 23-hectare central park just off Place Stanislas — a former tree nursery laid out in the 18th century, with shaded alleys, a rose garden, a small zoo, a bandstand and a Rodin statue of the painter Claude Lorrain. The city's favourite green space.

A much-loved combination of tropical aquarium and natural-history museum run with the University of Lorraine — reef tanks on the ground floor beneath galleries of zoology and taxidermy upstairs. A family fixture near the Pépinière.

Nancy's opera house on the corner of Place Stanislas, built by Joseph Hornecker of the École de Nancy and inaugurated in 1919, blending classical composition with Art Nouveau detail. One of France's national opera companies, worth seeing for the building alone.

Nancy's 18th-century cathedral in the Ville-Neuve, a monumental classical church built 1703-1742 with a grand organ and a rotunda painted by the Nancy artist Claude Jacquart — the seat of the diocese and a quieter counterpoint to the Art Nouveau and baroque sights.

sights.n: Chambre de Commerce et d'Industrie (Art Nouveau)
sights.w: One of the great built statements of the École de Nancy — the 1908 Chamber of Commerce building whose interior gathers stained glass, ironwork and marquetry by Nancy's Art Nouveau masters, including landscapes of Lorraine in glass. A highlight of the city's Art Nouveau trail.

Nancy's grand covered market in a U-shaped 1852 neoclassical hall between Place Charles III and Rue Saint-Dizier, with a glass-roofed 2017 courtyard added. More than sixty stalls of Lorraine produce — quiche, pâté lorrain, mirabelle, bergamote, the century-old Marchand cheese affineurs — plus counters to eat on the spot.

sights.address: Avenue du Maréchal Juin, 54000 Nancy, France
sights.w: A leafy 7.5-hectare public garden southwest of the centre, near the Art Nouveau villas of the Thermal quarter, with a magnolia classed a 'Remarkable Tree of France' and a pavilion from the 1909 international exhibition. A pleasant pairing with a Villa Majorelle walk.

sights.address: Place de la Cathédrale, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sights.w: The pink-sandstone Gothic masterpiece at the heart of the Grande Île, its single spire completed in 1439 and the tallest structure in Christendom until the 19th century. Inside, the 19th-century astronomical clock by Schwilgué springs to life daily at 12:30, and the platform gives a sweeping view over the city; entry to the church is free.

Strasbourg's historic core — the island bounded by the Ill, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1988 and extended in 2017 to take in the German-era Neustadt. Together they read as a lesson in European city-building, from the medieval Grande Île to the monumental Haussmann-meets-Germanic avenues of the imperial new town.

sights.address: Quai de la Petite France, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sights.w: The postcard quarter of the Grande Île — the former tanners' and fishermen's district, a maze of cobbled lanes and half-timbered houses from the 16th and 17th centuries leaning over the canals of the Ill, the most photographed being the galleried Maison des Tanneurs. Part of the UNESCO site.

sights.address: Quai de la Bruche, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sights.w: The medieval Covered Bridges with their three surviving watchtowers and, just upstream, the Barrage Vauban — a pink-sandstone dam-bridge built 1686-1690 to Vauban's plans, its terrace giving the classic panorama over Petite France. Part of the UNESCO Grande Île.

The former prince-bishops' palace beside the cathedral, an 18th-century masterpiece housing three museums under one roof — the Archaeological Museum, the Museum of Decorative Arts (with its sumptuous state apartments) and the Museum of Fine Arts. Strasbourg's grandest cultural address.

A folk-life museum of old Alsace spread through a warren of Renaissance timber-framed houses on the Ill — reconstructed interiors, painted furniture, costumes, ceramics and the everyday objects of pre-industrial rural Alsace, reached by creaking galleries and wooden staircases.

sights.address: 1 Place Hans Jean Arp, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sights.w: Strasbourg's big glass-roofed museum of modern and contemporary art beside the Barrage Vauban, strong on Kandinsky, Arp, Ernst and the Strasbourg-born abstraction of Jean Arp and Sophie Taeuber-Arp, with a rooftop café over Petite France.

The largest square of the city centre and its meeting point, named for the Strasbourg-born general Jean-Baptiste Kléber whose statue stands at the centre, framed by the 18th-century Aubette building. The city's giant Christmas tree stands here in Advent.

sights.n: Quartier européen – Parlement européen & Palais de l'Europe
sights.w: Strasbourg's identity as a European capital made visible: the European Parliament's 1999 hemicycle building, the Council of Europe's Palais de l'Europe (1977), the European Court of Human Rights and ARTE, gathered north of the Orangerie. The Parliament welcomes some 140,000 visitors a year.

Strasbourg's oldest and grandest park, laid out in the 18th century and remodelled by the landscape gardener of Napoleon III, opposite the European institutions — a lake with rowing boats, a small zoo and stork enclosure (the Alsatian emblem), and the Josephine pavilion. Free and much loved by locals.

The 'cathedral of Alsatian Protestantism' — a rare five-nave hall church, largely 13th-15th century, holding the monumental Baroque mausoleum of Marshal Maurice de Saxe by Pigalle and a Silbermann organ once played by Albert Schweitzer and Mozart.

sights.address: Place de la République, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sights.w: The monumental heart of the German-built Neustadt, a circular garden square ringed by grand imperial buildings — the Palais du Rhin, the National and University Library, the Théâtre National de Strasbourg and the Préfecture — and a keystone of the UNESCO extension.

sights.n: Musée Tomi Ungerer – Centre international de l'illustration
sights.address: 2 Avenue de la Marseillaise, 67000 Strasbourg, France
sights.w: France's first museum devoted to illustration, in a 19th-century villa near the Contades — 14,000 drawings by the Strasbourg-born artist Tomi Ungerer, from beloved children's books to biting satire and erotica, that he gave to his home city.

A hidden monument of the modern avant-garde: the leisure-complex interiors Theo van Doesburg, Hans Arp and Sophie Taeuber-Arp created in 1928 inside the 18th-century Aubette on Place Kléber — 'the Sistine Chapel of abstraction' — restored and reopened, and free to visit.

sights.address: Place du Général de Gaulle, 67700 Saverne, France
sights.w: The 'little Versailles of Alsace' — the vast 18th-century pink-sandstone palace of the prince-bishops of Strasbourg on the Marne-Rhine canal at Saverne, its 140 m garden facade one of the longest in France. Now a museum of archaeology, art and the writer-activist Louise Weiss. A gateway sight on the Nancy-Strasbourg corridor.

sights.n: Vitrail 'La Paix' de Chagall – Chapelle des Cordeliers, Sarrebourg
sights.w: Marc Chagall's monumental stained-glass window 'La Paix' (Peace), 12 m high, glowing in the deconsecrated Chapelle des Cordeliers at Sarrebourg, with the companion 'Paix' tapestry in the town museum — the highlight of a Chagall trail on the corridor between Nancy and Strasbourg.

sights.n: Obernai – cité médiévale & Place du Marché
sights.w: The second-most-visited town of the Bas-Rhin after Strasbourg — a walled Decapolis city at the foot of Mont Sainte-Odile whose market square gathers the 1554 Kornhalle grain hall, the 1523 town hall, the six-bucket Renaissance well and the 60 m Kapellturm belfry. A wine-road gateway rich in half-timbered houses.

Alsace's spiritual summit — a 763 m sandstone promontory crowned by the convent founded in the 7th century by St Odile, patron of Alsace, ringed by the mysterious prehistoric 'Mur Païen'. A pilgrimage and viewpoint drawing well over a million visitors a year, 15 minutes above Obernai.
